editorialPolicy: The Last Witness is an evolving fictionalized life story, not an evidence ledger. Quest, level, profession and location information informs internal continuity; do not mention screenshots, user reports, trackers, API responses, sources, or verification within the novel. Do not invent official quest completions, levels or visits; literary dialogue, emotions and ambience may be dramatized. Preserve established chronology and chapter anchors.

pages.chapter: Front matter
pages.title: To those history forgets
paragraphs: There are no monuments here for kings. No chronicles of victorious armies. These pages belong to the ones who passed unnoticed through rain, wheat and winter, whose names the world scarcely bothered to learn.
Xuthar Morvayne was not born with a prophecy. He was born with questions, and eventually he learned that even a question may become a burden when it asks too much of the living.

The world would call him many things before his journey was done: priest, wanderer, fool, perhaps even hero. This was not a book about the names others gave him. It was the story of the man who walked beneath them, carrying a memory that refused to die.

pages.chapter: Prologue · The Last Witness
pages.title: The things no one remembers
paragraphs: There are silences that belong to peace, and others that grow where a name should have been. For years I mistook the first for the second.

A woman died with my hand in hers. She did not ask to be spared. She asked not to disappear. I did not know her name. I have carried the shame of that ignorance longer than I carried her body from the room.
Now my bag contains little: a robe mended too often, a needle, a book whose pages refuse to remain empty and the uneasy possibility that something waits for me in the silence.
I shall not call it truth merely because it speaks. Somewhere beyond these walls are villages, roads and people who will never be written into history. I do not yet know where my own path begins.
If a life must end, let at least its name endure.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Before the road
pages.title: The house of missing names
paragraphs: The Morvaynes had never owned enough land to make their surname important. They had owned paper. In their narrow house, records leaned against the walls, tied with fraying strings: inventories of modest estates, petitions sent by uncertain hands, lists of the dead whose graves had never received a stone.

As a child, Xuthar thought the work tedious. A good story surely required a king, a battle, a victory. His mother corrected him one evening by placing an empty page beside the record of a life no one remembered. 'Which of these', she asked, 'will be easier for the world to forget?'
The boy did not answer. That was the first lesson he kept.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Before the road
pages.title: The lessons of light
paragraphs: In the care of priests shaped by Stormwind's teachings, he learned patience before he learned power. He tended lamps, memorized prayers and watched those who made themselves useful without expecting witnesses.

He loved the quiet mercy of healing. What troubled him was the certainty with which some spoke of the Light's will. He had seen the faithful remain unhealed. He had seen cruel men carried through sickness by accidents that looked like blessings. The questions gathered until they felt heavier than the books in his arms.
He did not turn against compassion. He turned against the comfort of pretending he knew why suffering had chosen one door and spared another.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The winter vigil
pages.title: The woman without a name
paragraphs: Snow whispered against the shutters that night. The dying woman in the narrow bed had no visitor. Xuthar had tried everything he knew, and now there was nothing left to offer but a chair and the refusal to leave.
She held his wrist. Her hand was astonishingly light. 'Do not pray that I will be saved,' she said. 'Pray that someone will remember I existed.'
The words remained after her breath did not. He waited for the familiar reassurance of the Light. Instead he found a silence so complete that it seemed to be listening back.
He did not know her name. That ignorance followed him farther than any road.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The winter vigil
pages.title: The first whisper
paragraphs: A thought arrived in the empty room: And who will remember her?

He could not say whether it came from exhaustion, grief or something beyond the reach of his education. He had read enough warnings about the Void to know that a voice capable of asking an honest question might still intend a dishonest end.
He lit a candle, wrote the woman's last words and left the space for her name empty. It was the only honest record he could make.
For the first time, his unanswered prayer had become a responsibility rather than an accusation.

pages.chapter: Chapter III · The ledger
pages.title: Written in a fading flame
paragraphs: Years later, among the family's damaged records, he found a book whose leaves looked untouched. A candle held close to the paper drew out delicate lines of ink that vanished when the flame moved away.

He tried again. The lines returned. Names, broken dates, accounts too brief to understand. He searched for a family history and found instead a list that appeared to have forgotten how to remain on the page.
Then he saw his own name. Beside it, no date of birth. Only a sentence: The last witness must not remember.
The words frightened him less than the possibility that he would believe them without proof.

pages.chapter: Chapter III · The ledger
pages.title: A road rather than an answer
paragraphs: He gathered the book, a needle, his travel-worn robes and what little money he could spare. He would investigate, not obey. A revelation that demanded surrender was not a revelation he meant to trust.

He decided to listen to people whose names would never become landmarks. He would keep records of campsites, old stories and small kindnesses. The Shadow would be a tool used with fear and care, never a master to whom he gave his judgment.
Before leaving, he wrote one rule on the inside cover: No answer is sacred enough to be spared a question.

pages.chapter: Chapter IV · The Night of the Gates
pages.title: Five hundred souls before the dawn
paragraphs: In the first hours of that November dawn, the gates of Azeroth seemed to hold a world of restless souls on the other side. Strangers had gathered from countless roads, each carrying a name, a hunger, a history not yet told. Xuthar Morvayne waited among them, a man of ink and unanswered prayers.

He had crossed no battlefield. His blade had tasted no blood. And yet he sensed the curious weight of a beginning: the knowledge that an ordinary moment, once lived, could never be lived for the first time again.

The old ledger rested, in the story he carried within himself, beneath his travelling robes. Its warning had not changed: The last witness must not remember. He had chosen, against that command, to remember everything.

When the way opened, he went forward with the others. Some were searching for glory, some for fellowship, some only for another place to begin. Xuthar sought a life in which no name was too small to remember.

pages.chapter: Chapter IV · The Night of the Gates
pages.title: A name spoken into the world
paragraphs: He stood in pale robes edged in blue, with auburn braids falling against his shoulders and a weathered face beneath a stubborn brow. Xuthar Morvayne. At last the letters were no longer a name reserved on a page: they belonged to a living traveller standing on Azeroth's threshold.

Beyond the stone and rooftops lay the first blue of morning. It was too gentle a sky for prophecies. No thunder proclaimed him chosen; no host of angels knelt. There was only the quiet uncertainty that attends the first step.

A lesser chronicle might have called it the birth of a hero. Xuthar would have objected. Heroes were remembered for victories. He had come to learn how the forgotten survived the world's indifference.
And then, without ceremony, he entered.

pages.chapter: Chapter V · The Abbey of a Thousand Voices
pages.title: Northshire did not sleep
paragraphs: He expected the Abbey of Northshire to greet him with bells, stone corridors and the discipline of early prayer. Instead, a sea of bodies surged across its green approaches. Travellers called out to one another; names floated above every head like banners in a wind no one else could see.

Some laughed. Some shouted that they had made it. Others stood as if afraid that moving would break the spell of arrival. A thousand private destinies collided beneath the same innocent sky, and for one impossible instant the world seemed to hold its breath around them.
Xuthar listened. A nameless crowd, his old teachers might have called it. But he had never believed in nameless crowds. There were only people whose names had not yet been learned.
He could scarcely see the road beneath their feet. It was not the solemn entrance imagined by a pilgrim. It was far better: the ungovernable, human music of a world beginning again.

pages.chapter: Chapter V · The Abbey of a Thousand Voices
pages.title: The humblest of vows
paragraphs: Beyond the excitement lay the ordinary labour of Northshire: requests from neighbours, vermin in the fields, wolves among the grass, a marshal attempting to hold a troubled valley together with too few hands.

Xuthar was no master of shadow here. His power was young, his purse light, his knowledge incomplete. He could offer no grand miracle. What he could offer was his attention and the strength of two untested hands.
An old thought returned to him: the world is not saved only by those whose names are carved into stone. Sometimes it is kept alive by the person who answers when another calls for help.
So he went into the fields. The first deeds of his chronicle would be smaller than legends, and therefore, perhaps, more worthy of being told.

pages.chapter: Chapter VI · Teeth Beneath the Green
pages.title: The wolves of the first morning
paragraphs: In the grass beyond the abbey, the first wolves waited. Nothing in their eyes resembled evil. They were hungry creatures, born into the same uncertain world as the man approaching them. Yet their teeth were real, and the danger they posed required an answer.

At the second measure of his growing strength, Xuthar faced them with the little magic a novice priest could command. Each encounter left the pulse beating hard in his throat. Each victory taught him how fragile a mortal body remained beneath a sacred robe.
He did not mistake survival for mastery. If anything, the struggle unsettled him: the Light could warm a dying hand, yet the same disciplined will could turn prayer towards violence.
Somewhere in his memory, the woman from the winter vigil asked that she not be forgotten. He carried her silence into the fields, and walked on.

pages.chapter: Chapter VI · Teeth Beneath the Green
pages.title: Marshal McBride's summons
paragraphs: By the time Xuthar returned beneath Northshire's ancient stone, he had reached the third level of his apprenticeship. Marshal McBride waited near the abbey's threshold, a soldier whose work allowed little room for mystery and less for hesitation.

The danger among the kobolds had been driven back, and McBride offered the novice his first hard-earned thanks. More work followed: a hallowed letter bearing the familiar weight of his calling, and a troubling request to investigate Echo Ridge. The name of that place seemed to hang in the air long after it was spoken.

Xuthar sought out the priestly trainer. There was comfort in the familiar gravity of the abbey, but no escape from the questions that had brought him there. A lesson could teach the shape of an incantation; it could not tell a man what his power ought to mean.
He left the quiet halls with a clearer road before him, not a clearer answer.

pages.chapter: Chapter VII · Where the Earth Remembers
pages.title: The road to Echo Ridge
paragraphs: North of the monastery, the green earth darkened beneath towering trees. At Echo Ridge the cobolds laboured in the shadow of the slopes, digging and scuttling among rough camps. Their fires were small; the forest around them was vast.

Xuthar followed the work of an ordinary commission into a place that felt older than the abbey bells. The first kobold workers fell, not to a triumphant champion but to a novice learning to stand his ground. Beneath the roots, the earth yielded fragments of stolen books, mute witnesses to other hands and other lives.

He wondered who had owned them. A prayer book, perhaps; a merchant's ledger; a child's account of a summer that would never come again. The contents were still unknown, but the question itself was enough to make him bend and gather what he could.
From somewhere among the trees came the faint crackle of a cooking fire. The valley had ceased to be a starting zone. It had become a place with its own terrible, ordinary needs.

pages.chapter: Chapter VII · Where the Earth Remembers
pages.title: The chronicle remains unfinished
paragraphs: Echo Ridge was not done with him. There were still kobold workers at the edge of the mine, still stolen books hidden among the roots, still dangerous men in red cloth farther across the valley. He had recovered a few pieces of what was missing, but an unfinished task had a way of growing heavier in the mind.

He stood among the roots and dark grass at level three, the abbey behind him and the promise of unknown roads ahead. Nothing in the scene would have persuaded a passing stranger that history had begun to turn. There was no crown, no dragon, no empire falling beneath a blade.

But in a quieter chronicle, the measure of a life is different. A man who had sworn to preserve forgotten names had taken his first steps among people and creatures whom greater histories would overlook.
The night had opened its gates. The first pages were written. Beyond Echo Ridge, the unwritten world waited.

pages.chapter: Chapter VII · Where the Earth Remembers
pages.title: What Echo Ridge Did Not Tell
paragraphs: The mouth of Echo Ridge Mine seemed to breathe with another creature's lungs. Xuthar heard the tapping of picks before he saw torchlight, a restless music of stone and fear in the dark.

From the mouth of the mine, the earth seemed to breathe with another creature's lungs. Xuthar heard the tapping of picks before he saw the flicker of torchlight. The kobolds had dug passages beneath a mountain that no longer felt certain of itself, and the darkness gave back every sound twice.

A younger priest might have called the place a nest of monsters. Xuthar could not ignore the buckets, the tired tools, the hurried marks scratched into the stone. Fear and cruelty were not the same thing, although fear could become cruel when it held a weapon. The road had asked him to oppose the threat; his journal asked him what had caused it.

At the last bend, where the mine narrowed into shadow, he touched his finger to a seam of cold rock. He imagined the mountain remembering every hand that had struck it. He had come to drive danger away from Northshire. He left with a more troubling question: who would remember those who had never learned any other home?
And in the book he carried beside the cloth and the needle, he wrote: 'An echo is only a voice the world has refused to let die.'

pages.chapter: Chapter VII · Where the Earth Remembers
pages.title: The Silence between the Pines
paragraphs: At Northshire Abbey, the first great crowd slowly loosened into individual journeys. Xuthar remembered the faces he had passed, the restless voices, the wolves stirring beyond the green, and the first summons that brought him before Marshal McBride. A letter awaited him, bearing the familiar demands of his calling. The road to Echo Ridge waited too.

There were books missing in the woods and kobold workers beneath the earth. Some of the scattered pages had found their way into his hands; others still lay beyond his reach. Red-clad thieves troubled the fields farther off, their insignia a warning against the illusion that all dangers walked on four legs.

The priest returned his attention to the ledger. One name could be written in a heartbeat, but learning the story beneath it might take a lifetime. He closed the cover on an unfinished day, knowing the valley would ask him to begin again.

pages.chapter: Chapter VIII · Red Cloth Beneath the Trees
pages.title: Men beneath the dark boughs
paragraphs: Beyond the safer paths of Northshire, the fields lay beneath the long shadows of ancient trees. The land still bore the patient furrows of honest hands, but the men who watched those furrows had come with other intentions. Defias thugs stood among the fences, their red insignia as stark as wounds against the green.

Xuthar halted before the first of them. Until now he had struggled against hunger given the shape of a wolf, or against the restless labour of kobolds beneath a hill. These were men. Their anger had a history; their threats could be understood in words. That knowledge did not make them harmless.

The novice priest felt his heartbeat climb, yet he did not turn away. He had reached the fifth step of his growing strength, and the world was already asking whether his compassion could survive the need to resist another human being.

In the thick of the struggle, a Defias thug and two companions pressed him so hard that he escaped with scarcely six heartbeats of strength left in a hundred. The woods became very quiet then. He leaned against a tree, felt the blood beating in his ears, and wondered whether survival always sounded so much like fear.
Above the fields, the branches moved like dark fingers against the sky. No voice announced the correct path. The choice, like all the difficult choices to come, belonged to him.

pages.chapter: Chapter VIII · Red Cloth Beneath the Trees
pages.title: Twelve tokens of a broken brotherhood
paragraphs: The fight was not the stuff of tavern songs. There were no royal trumpets, no sweeping banners, no triumphant charge. There was only the rhythm of danger, the need to hold one enemy at a time, and the bitter knowledge that a priest's hands could be called upon for violence.

The red burlap bandanas were proof of the work entrusted to him. Twelve had been required to answer the Brotherhood of Thieves, and twelve now lay in his care. What reward might follow mattered less than the troubled fields behind him, where ordinary people had learned to mistrust strangers in red.

He regarded those scraps of cloth and wondered what oath had once made the brotherhood worthy of its name. Men could bind themselves together for justice or for cruelty. Sometimes the difference became visible only to those standing in the path of their weapons.
He had won no great war in that shadowed field. Yet he had learned something that a hundred sheltered sermons could scarcely teach: the darkest deeds were not always born of darkness alone.

pages.chapter: Chapter IX · The Abbey's Vigil
pages.title: The long road back to silence
paragraphs: When he returned to Northshire Abbey, the world had not become less troubled. Beyond its walls the forest still concealed unfinished errands, and beyond the forest lay an immeasurable continent of unanswered names. Yet within the stone halls there was room for a quieter kind of courage.

The candles did not ask how many foes he had faced. The worn benches did not weigh his victories. Here, among ordinary walls and the traces of a thousand prayers, Xuthar could cease for a moment to be a combatant and remember the simple burden of being alive.

He rested. His level had risen to five, and the work against the Defias was done, but he felt no compulsion to outrun the next sunrise. The road would remain. Nothing important would be lost by listening to the silence between one adventure and another.

In that pause the priest understood, perhaps for the first time, that a chronicle was not made only of battles. Someone must also preserve the moments in which a weary traveller lays down his burdens and decides to begin again.

pages.chapter: Chapter IX · The Abbey's Vigil
pages.title: A candle between Light and Shadow
paragraphs: A single candle trembled in the abbey's half-light. In its gold Xuthar saw the teachings that had carried him this far: patience, mercy, the insistence that even the smallest life deserved a witness. Around it waited the shadow, neither friend nor enemy, only the great unknown that made the little flame visible.

He remembered the old family records, the dying stranger whose name he had never learned, and the words that appeared beneath the ledger's fading ink. The last witness must not remember. There was an almost cruel humour in that warning. All he wanted was to remember.

Outside, Azeroth moved on without him. The world was enormous; his adventures, so far, scarcely filled a valley. But he was no longer the man who had stood at the threshold, wondering whether he belonged among the thousands who had arrived.
He closed his eyes, not to escape the road but to honour the distance already walked. Tomorrow could ask its questions. Tonight, the answer was rest.

pages.chapter: Chapter IX · The Abbey's Vigil
pages.title: The Cost of Twelve Red Ribbons
paragraphs: The red bandanas lay together like the remnants of some ill-starred festival. Twelve tokens taken from men who had made fear their trade. Xuthar could recall how close the fight had brought him to the edge: one desperate retreat had left him with scarcely any strength to stand. It was an ugly kind of lesson, and he had learned it without applause.

Back at the Abbey, his thoughts turned from the Defias to the unfinished work among the kobolds. The mine still demanded a reckoning; the stolen books still called for patient hands. Deputy Willem's modest reward and the weight of a militia hammer were almost absurd beside the enormity of the world outside.

He rested beneath stone that had endured longer than any one life. Five stages of learning had brought him here, but he could feel how little they amounted to. He thought of those who had sent him into danger, and of those who never learned whether the messenger returned.
A candle burned down on the nearest table. In its dwindling light the shadows seemed less like enemies than questions, and Xuthar had always been more afraid of easy answers.

pages.chapter: Chapter IX · The Abbey's Vigil
pages.title: The Valley of Many Beginnings
paragraphs: Northshire had been a multitude before it became a place. At the Abbey gate the gathered travellers called out in disbelief at their own arrival. By the time Xuthar ventured toward the timber wolves and the kobold camps, the shouting had faded behind him, replaced by the rustle of leaves and the hard scrape of desperate work.

Marshal McBride gave him reasons to return and new reasons to leave. Deputy Willem, who stood where the road met the Abbey's protection, knew the names of local threats as a farmer knows the names of storms. A priest might carry a hallowed letter in one pocket and a worn weapon in the other; neither promised that the next bend would be kind.

He passed fenced plots and glimpsed Defias men where ordinary labour should have been safe. Their scarves were red, and the fields had begun to fear that colour. The stolen books from Echo Ridge seemed suddenly part of the same story: people taking what did not belong to them, then expecting the world to become accustomed to the loss.

By the time he reached the Abbey again, Xuthar had crossed from the first nervous strength of a novice to the greater weariness of a man who had fought and survived. He did not know all the names of those who had travelled beside him. That ignorance, more than his bruises, troubled him.

pages.chapter: Chapter X · Letters and Unfinished Harvests
pages.title: Promises Waiting at the Abbey Gate
paragraphs: Some errands end when the last enemy falls. Others begin only then. The threat of Echo Ridge had been answered in part, and the valley had its own questions about the work that remained. Xuthar found himself moving between the Abbey's familiar walls and the fields where neighbours had learned to count on small acts of courage.

Milly's harvest lay under the threat of thieves. Garrick Padfoot had made himself a name whispered with anger. Farther away, a priestess awaited a young traveller whose faith had already acquired fractures. Xuthar carried these obligations without pretending they were equal; hunger, justice and belief each weighed differently on the heart.

He looked out from the old stone toward the green country beyond. The paths branched like lines in a palm. Not every promise could be fulfilled in the same hour, but all of them had been made to somebody. That was reason enough not to forget.

pages.chapter: Chapter X · Letters and Unfinished Harvests
pages.title: The Names Beyond the Abbey
paragraphs: The Abbey of Northshire had not yet released Xuthar from its quiet obligations. Beneath the shelter of stone and tree, the smallest errands waited with the patience of unwritten vows. Someone had gathered the harvest that Milly had feared lost. Elsewhere, Garrick Padfoot's name remained upon a bounty; the task's objective was complete, though no reward had yet been shown.

And now the world was asking him to carry words rather than to wield them. Marshal McBride had documents intended for Marshal Dughan in Goldshire. Near that same settlement, Sam Sarsparilla awaited an adventurer. Beyond the abbey's stables waited Tordrin Sternblade; somewhere in Elwynn Forest, Priestess Josetta stood at the far end of a road of faith.

No triumphant trumpet sounded above these new assignments. Some wanted a conversation, some a message delivered, others a duty acknowledged. Xuthar, who had spent the night learning how often a life could be forgotten, began to understand that a name written on an errand could be the beginning of a stranger's story.

Beyond Northshire lay Goldshire, its people still strangers and its roofs only a promise on the road. The letters waited in his bag, and Xuthar knew better than to mistake a long pause for the end of a journey. Every road begins before the traveller takes it.

pages.chapter: Chapter X · Letters and Unfinished Harvests
pages.title: Four Names Beyond Northshire
paragraphs: The vineyards had demanded his attention, as had the outlaw Garrick. By the time Xuthar stood again among Northshire's old stones, the worst of those immediate burdens had begun to loosen. A harvest could be returned to the people who tended it; a frightened valley could believe, briefly, that justice had not entirely deserted the road.

New names waited beyond the shelter of the Abbey. Sam Sarsparilla was to be found near Goldshire. Marshal Dughan awaited documents from McBride. Tordrin Sternblade had business with the kobold trails, and Priestess Josetta waited somewhere farther along the path of the Light. To another traveller these might have seemed a dreary chain of errands. To Xuthar, each name opened a door onto a life not yet understood.
He tucked the papers against his chest. Paper had always been his family's burden. Now he began to suspect it might also be his way through the world.

pages.chapter: Chapter XI · The Measure of a Journey
pages.title: Six Steps beneath an Unwritten Sky
paragraphs: Some journeys announce themselves with the roar of dragons or the fall of a king. Xuthar Morvayne's sixth milestone was quieter. A novice priest, once lost among the countless names outside Northshire Abbey, had found the strength to take one more step across a world vast enough to swallow legends.

He thought of the wolves in the dark grass, the kobolds beneath Echo Ridge and the red-clad men haunting the fields. Each had taught him something different about fear. But the living world offered lessons beyond combat: names to remember, letters to carry, strangers waiting patiently for a word.

During those days the name Sandriana crossed his path in Elwynn. He saw her more than once, a figure moving through the same immense woodland without asking to become part of his fate. Xuthar had learned to treasure such glimpses. The world was made not only of companions, but of lives that brushed against one's own and went on.

Goldshire still waited farther along the road. The old ledger offered no prophecy of what lay beyond the abbey. It offered only an empty page and the solemn freedom to fill it when the next day arrived.
At level six, Xuthar was neither master of Light nor child of Shadow. He was simply a man who had begun—and who chose to keep going.

pages.chapter: Chapter XII · The Earth Remembers
pages.title: The Unwritten Trail
paragraphs: The Abbey's old stones had taught Xuthar the weight of silence. The woodland earth, it seemed, could teach him something else. There were marks in the soil, slight and restless, and somewhere in their crooked pattern lay the promise of a story no human scribe had yet written.

He followed the slight disturbances left by the kobolds, searching for six marks that might reveal where they had passed. No champion's blade was needed to read what the ground had kept, only patience, attention and the willingness to kneel where others would stride past.

Beyond the valley waited names he had yet to know: Sam Sarsparilla, Marshal Dughan and Priestess Josetta. Goldshire beckoned with those unfinished encounters. He carried their names beside his own, as though remembering a stranger might already be the beginning of helping them.
A witness must first learn to look, he wrote in the margin of the old book. The words looked plain enough. He wondered how many years it would take to understand them.

pages.chapter: Chapter XII · The Earth Remembers
pages.title: Writing in the Soil
paragraphs: A broken twig, a bruise in the moss, a small mark pressed into damp soil: the kobolds left their own language behind them. Xuthar had been trained to interpret holy texts, but these signs required no doctrine, only the humility to look closely.

Beyond the last trail lay the broader world of Elwynn. The road toward Goldshire promised messages to deliver, a marshal to find and a priestess whose questions might be harder to answer than those of a soldier. He followed the marks slowly, unwilling to trade attention for speed.
The old ledger in his satchel contained page upon page of names. It had never taught him to hear a footstep after the foot had gone. That was a lesson the forest offered freely.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIII · Six Signs and a Distant Lantern
pages.title: The Trail Falls Silent
paragraphs: The forest had guarded its secret beneath roots and fallen leaves, but six hidden signs had finally been found. Xuthar could return with the answer entrusted to him. There was no trumpet, no ceremonial procession, only the soft certainty that attention had won where impatience would have failed.

Beyond the dark woodland, the road spoke of another kind of refuge. At the Lion's Pride Inn, an innkeeper named Farley awaited a visitor. Somewhere in the same wider world, Sam Sarsparilla, Marshal Dughan and Priestess Josetta waited for words, documents or the footsteps of a travelling priest.

He imagined warmth behind the tavern's windows: bread, voices, the ordinary mercy of a roof against the weather. The thought was enough to set him moving. One could follow a trail for duty, but sometimes a man followed the road simply because he was tired of being cold.

The road ahead would not vanish because he paused to study it. Somewhere beyond Northshire stood Goldshire, with its unanswered invitations and the first possibility of feeling, for one evening, less like a stranger in an immense new world.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIII · Six Signs and a Distant Lantern
pages.title: When the Trail Gives Up Its Secret
paragraphs: Six signs lay behind him now. What had begun as nearly invisible scratches in the woodland had become a path he could follow, its meaning no longer buried beneath leaves. He had not needed a grand revelation. He had needed patience and enough daylight to keep searching.

Beyond the trees another kind of promise awaited him. Goldshire, with its timbered roofs and warm hearths, called to the part of him that was simply tired. At the Lion's Pride Inn stood a man named Farley, keeper of beds, meals and the temporary peace that strangers buy with honest coin.

There were letters still to carry and names still to seek. Xuthar tightened his satchel and started toward the village. The tracks in the forest could wait for another day; for once, his own footsteps mattered more.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIV · What the Earth Can Teach
pages.title: Leaves, Fire and Unwritten Roads
paragraphs: The forests around Elwynn had so far taught Xuthar to listen for danger: wolves beneath the trees, kobolds between the roots, men whose intentions were as sharp as their blades. Yet the green world guarded quieter teachings as well. Not every useful thing drawn from the earth was meant to harm another living soul.

Two unfamiliar disciplines now called to him. Herbalism offered the patient study of plants; cooking promised the art of taking what the earth gave and making it sustaining. Tomas, in Goldshire, knew the language of the hearth. Xuthar was only beginning to understand how much he had to learn.

It pleased him, perhaps, that the same hands which summoned holy fire might someday crush a leaf to preserve life or prepare an evening's meal. There was dignity in a meal shared after a hard road and in the patient knowledge of a plant's name. Even a witness needed to eat, to heal, and to learn what grew beside the paths he walked.

Farley at the Lion's Pride Inn, Marshal Dughan and Priestess Josetta waited somewhere beyond the paths he knew. Goldshire was close enough that he could almost picture its chimneys. He looked toward the trees, and the road did not hurry him.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIV · What the Earth Can Teach
pages.title: Two Lessons for Mortal Hands
paragraphs: It had taken surprisingly little time for Xuthar to discover how much a priest must know beyond prayer. A road was not always a test of courage. Sometimes it asked for fire, food, clean bandages and an understanding of the leaves growing at one's feet.

He considered the quiet disciplines of herbalism and cooking. Tomas, in Goldshire, knew what could be made from an ordinary hearth; the woodland knew the names of plants to anyone patient enough to learn them. Those pursuits sounded modest beside the dangers of Echo Ridge, but Xuthar could not call them unimportant.
He had watched people die with prayers on their lips. What use was faith, he wondered, if it had no hands with which to mend a sleeve, feed the hungry or prepare a place to rest?

pages.chapter: Chapter XV · The Sun beyond the Abbey
pages.title: Where the Lion Watches
paragraphs: The morning had changed its colour. Where once the forest had hung above Xuthar in folds of dark green, sunlight now poured through its branches like molten gold. He stood upon the threshold of the abbey, at the place where the old lion watched over water and stone, and felt the world stretch far beyond the walls that had sheltered his first uncertain prayers.

The name Garrick Padfoot had passed from an unfinished summons into a deed accomplished. The outlaw would trouble the valley no more, and the novice had crossed another threshold in his growing strength. McBride's thanks were modest; the relief of those living along the road mattered far more.

Another document travelled with him now: a Grape Manifest, a humble list that must find its way to Brother Neals. He had learned that the world was stitched together less by prophecies than by errands entrusted from one mortal hand to another. Each name in the task book was a door. Most had yet to open.

Beyond the archway, the road through Elwynn curled beneath immense trees. The cobblestones held the day's warmth. Strangers passed in the opposite direction; from somewhere unseen came the faint rhythm of a settlement going about its business. He followed the road because the world, at last, was asking him to travel rather than merely survive.

Goldshire appeared not as a fortress of heroes but as a place people had built to live in. Blue roofs rose above timbered walls; a chimney leaned above the street; a horse waited by the stables. Between the buildings lay sunlight, conversation, and the promise of a doorway left open.

Xuthar paused in the village road. He had reached a place full of other people's lives, and there was no need to lay claim to them all at once. He listened to a stable door opening, a distant voice near the square, the patient splash of water. To know a place, he suspected, one must first allow it to remain itself.

Thus did the first road out of Northshire find its destination. No crown was placed upon his brow. No dark god stirred in its sleep. Yet the world had become larger, and in the growing light, the young priest could feel the quiet beginning of another chapter.

pages.chapter: Chapter XV · The Sun beyond the Abbey
pages.title: The Lion at the Threshold
paragraphs: Garrick Padfoot's reign of petty terror had ended. It did not make Xuthar proud in the way old ballads described pride. He thought instead of the people who could walk their own fields without listening for a cutthroat at every fence.

The grape manifest remained a small, stubborn symbol of all the labour the Defias had tried to erase. He carried it toward the Abbey as carefully as he might carry an injured bird. Farther along waited the road to Goldshire, bright beneath the trees, watched over by a stone lion and a fountain whose waters went on falling regardless of human trouble.

The roofs of Goldshire emerged in blue and silver. Stables, chimneys and walls stood in the sunlight. Xuthar slowed, letting the sounds of the village reach him one by one. A new place had opened before him, and he did not yet know which of its people would remain in his memory.

pages.chapter: Chapter XV · The Sun beyond the Abbey
pages.title: The Harvest the Thieves Could Not Keep
paragraphs: The Northshire vineyards should have been a place of patient seasons. Instead the furrows carried the nervous silence of people who had learned to look for red bandanas between the vines.

Northshire Vineyards should have smelled of summer, even in November. The vines held the memory of ripening fruit in their empty branches. Between the rows, people had learned to walk quietly, because the Defias had begun to mistake every man's labour for something they were owed.

Milly did not ask Xuthar to become a hero. She asked whether he knew what it meant to watch a season disappear into someone else's hands. He thought of the monastery ledgers, of names recorded without their hunger or weariness. He promised no miracle. He only told her that a harvest deserved to belong to the hands that had tended it.

The grape manifest seemed an absurdly small conclusion to such trouble: an inventory, a signature, an ordinary piece of paper. Yet when it reached its proper destination, Xuthar imagined that it carried more than fruit. It carried proof that a woman had worked, that her work had mattered, and that a gang of thieves had not managed to erase her.
At dusk he closed the ledger without writing the thieves' names first. This was Milly's story. Let her name stand at the beginning.

pages.chapter: Chapter XVI · The Quiet Mercy of Fire
pages.title: The Inn Where Time Stood Still
paragraphs: He had thought the road ended where the roofs of Goldshire rose between the trees. But a village was not the end of a journey. It was an invitation: a hundred ordinary lives gathered beneath timber and slate, each carrying a story the world would never consider worthy of a chronicle.

When Xuthar entered the Lion's Pride Inn, the first thing he met was warmth. Firelight breathed from a wide red-brick hearth. Beneath heavy dark beams, candle flames trembled above weathered tables; barrels slept along the walls and glass bottles caught the glow as though some small stars had fallen to earth.

There was no battle to be fought inside those walls. Instead there were people whose trades gave the place its name and purpose: Farley, the innkeeper; Melika Isenstrider among the chairs; Dobbins behind the bar; Brog Hamfist keeping his goods within reach. They were not the kind of names sung by bards. That was precisely why the Last Witness would remember them.

Xuthar approached Farley, the keeper of the threshold between the dangerous road and the safety of a borrowed roof. The innkeeper had the practised stillness of a man who had seen every kind of weary traveller come through his door. Xuthar found comfort in that unremarkable welcome.

A little farther within, the room changed its voice. The wood creaked beneath his boots, and the warmth deepened around a working hearth. Tomas, a cook, stood by the kitchen fire; Toddrick the butcher laboured among ordinary provisions. Xuthar thought of how much there was to learn from hands that kept a town fed, even when the hands of warriors received all the praise.
Then, at last, he sat.

No triumph was announced. No chorus of soldiers hailed his return. The chair was plain, the company mixed, the air heavy with smoke, bread and the imagined murmur of conversations whose words he could not make out. His travelling robes fell still against the worn floorboards, and beside him rested the silence he had brought from Northshire.

For a moment he allowed his thoughts to wander toward every small life outside the inn: a farmhand beneath the trees, a merchant counting coins, a stranger taking the same forest road for the first time. Each would one day be forgotten by someone. Xuthar could not save them all from that fate. Perhaps he could, at least, refuse to let their stories vanish without a witness.

The flames shifted in their grate. Goldshire continued breathing around him. And for the first time since the gates of Forever had opened, the Last Witness gave himself permission to do nothing but rest.
There would be roads again. There would be shadows. But not yet.

pages.chapter: Chapter XVI · The Quiet Mercy of Fire
pages.title: The People Who Kept the Hearth
paragraphs: The Lion's Pride Inn had its own order of life. Farley kept watch over the arriving travellers; Melika moved among the tables, and Dobbins worked behind the bar. Brog Hamfist's provisions promised the sort of practical rescue a tired adventurer might need more urgently than a blessing.

In the kitchen the fire was a different creature. Tomas worked near the place where bread and broth could return strength to the living, while Toddrick stood among the plain necessities of a butcher's craft. Xuthar lingered there, struck by how much of a village's safety depended on people no ballad would ever celebrate.
Later he found a chair in the common room. The great brick hearth gave warmth without asking what wars he had survived. When he sat, his shoulders finally remembered their weariness.

He had crossed a valley of wolves, mines and thieves to reach this ordinary room. It seemed to him then that an inn was a kind of mercy: a place that did not demand to know who you had been before it gave you shelter.

pages.chapter: Chapter XVII · The Mercy of Water
pages.title: A Blessing at the Water's Edge
paragraphs: In Elwynn Forest, the road did not hurry its travellers. There were strangers sitting together around a campfire, their names flickering above the cobbles like little flags carried through the woodland.

Water opened between wooded banks; beside a tree waited Guard Roberts. The priest had come to learn that tending another person could be a kind of courage, even when the right words were difficult to find.

The trial known as Garments of the Light had taught him that care could falter through the smallest misjudgement. He returned to the precise prayer, the gentler touch of Lesser Heal, and at last completed what had been asked of him. The Friar's Robes of the Light became his reward; with them came another step forward in his apprenticeship, the seventh.

They were the first finely wrought green robes that the road had brought him. Around the same time he acquired a Book Bag, so perfectly suited to his strange vocation that it almost seemed a quiet jest of fate: the keeper of forgotten names had been given another place to carry words.
For Xuthar, the lesson was more enduring than the robe or the reward: mercy was not merely an ideal written in scripture. It was a prayer chosen with care, and a living person on the other end of it.

pages.chapter: Chapter XVII · The Mercy of Water
pages.title: The Light That Did Not Demand Belief
paragraphs: The robe lay folded across his hands. There was nothing extraordinary in the cloth itself, and yet the gift seemed to ask a question the priest had carried for years: could a man doubt the Light and still serve its mercy?

The robe did not feel like a victory. It was only cloth, carefully made, and yet its seams seemed to demand that Xuthar remember what he had once believed. He had learned to question the promises of the Light, but he had not forgotten how to answer another person's pain.

He recalled the lesson as though it were spoken beside a quiet hearth: heal first; ask about deserving later. No revelation had descended to reward him. No prophecy had named him necessary. What remained was the smaller, harder discipline of kindness without certainty.

His new garment was green by the reckoning of adventurers. To Xuthar it was the colour of the space between two convictions. He could wear it without surrendering his doubts, just as he could keep his needle and repair a tear without claiming to repair the world.
That night, beneath the fold of the robe, he wrote a single line in his journal: 'Mercy has never asked me to be right. It only asks that I do not turn away.'

pages.chapter: Chapter XVIII · Where the Mine Swallows Light
pages.title: Two Falls Beneath the Earth
paragraphs: The sunlit woods gave way to Fargodeep Mine, where supports and rough carts divided the dark into narrow strips. Kobold Miners moved through the passages, and a Rumbler troubled the depths. Their strength was written in the way the earth seemed to shake around them.

Twice the mine overwhelmed him. The first fall left the cold taste of helplessness in his mouth; the second came before he had learned how to bear the first. He discovered that even a priest could not speak his way out of every darkness.

Yet there had been narrow escapes as well: a Kobold Tunneler on one path, a Miner on another, each leaving him with scarcely a heartbeat of strength. He learned the difference between courage and the foolishness of staying one moment too long.

He had come seeking candles, gold dust and missing books. Some lay already in his bag, others still beyond his grasp, guarded by creatures who did not care what names he had written in his ledger. Each step farther into the mine meant weighing the cost of one more errand against the value of getting home alive.
Defeat left its marks on him, though none could be seen beneath the robe. He did not erase them from memory. A life told only through victories would be a dishonest life.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIX · Lanterns of the Capital
pages.title: The Road to Stormwind
paragraphs: After the mine, stone replaced soil. A torchlit passage opened on the streets of Stormwind; high timbered buildings faced the cobbles, and the Trade District buzzed with the ordinary business of people who had never seen a hero arrive.

At Morgan Pestle's door the small shipment of candles finally found the hands for which it had been intended. The errand brought him a modest reward, a little favour in the eyes of Stormwind and the strange satisfaction of having carried a promise safely across the road. He had grown stronger too; by the time the city opened around him, he had reached the eighth stage of his journey.

Later he walked beside the canals, pausing at the edge of a wooden dock where the water held the city upside down. Fishing teachers and passers-by moved somewhere behind him. He watched the reflections instead, thinking of all the names hidden by the windows above.

He wondered whether a city could truly remember the people who kept it alive. He had seen crowds around a fire, a guard beside the water, dangers underground, and now lanterns reflected from stone. There was more here to witness than victory.

Stormwind offered errands as numerous as its streets. A wine shop needed attention; the Jasperlode Mine waited beyond the walls; rare books were still missing; Guard Thomas awaited word; the teachings of herbalism had not yet settled into habit. Xuthar let their names rest in his thoughts as the light changed over the Trade District.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIX · Lanterns of the Capital
pages.title: Candles for a Distant Window
paragraphs: Before the great towers of Stormwind rose into view, Xuthar had already learned the worth of a humble errand. A small parcel of candles was enough to make him responsible for someone else's waiting night.

The roads between Goldshire and Stormwind were full of grander things than a box of candles: rumours of soldiers, merchants counting their losses, priests hurrying toward promises they could not keep. Xuthar carried his small parcel without ceremony. Somewhere in the city, Morgan was waiting for a shipment that another person had not been able to deliver.

The box had no gold seal. Nothing about its contents suggested destiny. That was precisely why he guarded it so carefully. In a world where every war asked for the sacrifice of ordinary people, the ordinary errand was a quiet act of resistance.

As the towers appeared beyond the last stretch of road, he pictured windows lighting one by one. A candle could not reveal every truth. It could not hold back the Shadow forever. But it might give a stranger enough time to finish a letter, or mend a sleeve, or remember a home they were afraid of forgetting.
When his footsteps crossed the stone of Stormwind, Xuthar did not imagine a triumphal procession. He imagined one small flame placed on a table, and another night made bearable.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIX · Lanterns of the Capital
pages.title: A City of Small Miracles
paragraphs: The capital greeted him with shopfronts, stone bridges and water as dark as polished glass. For the first time in days, Xuthar could walk among hundreds of lives without the forest pressing close about him. He had reached the eighth measure of his growing skill, but the city made every achievement seem small.

The priest's trial had given him the Friar's Robes of the Light, and a parcel of candles had brought him to Morgan Pestle. Neither event resembled the turning of an age. To Xuthar, however, there was something astonishing about arriving at the place where an ordinary stranger expected him.

He passed the canals and the wooden docks where anglers worked beneath the city walls. Somewhere close by, books and modest rewards changed hands. There were more errands than daylight, more names than paper, more ways to spend a life than any one traveller could follow.
The water beneath the bridges reflected the lamps in fragments. Xuthar leaned over the edge and wondered how many of those lights would still be burning when he returned.

pages.chapter: Chapter XIX · Lanterns of the Capital
pages.title: The Narrow Margins of Survival
paragraphs: Of the first eight stages of his journey, Xuthar remembered the near defeats more vividly than his successes. Once, among Defias blades in the vineyards, he had fled with scarcely a breath left in his lungs. Later, within Fargodeep's cramped passageways, two separate encounters left him one heartbeat from collapse.

The mine itself had taken him down twice. That was not a detail he wished to conceal. He remembered the helplessness of defeat and the humiliating discovery that pride could not keep a living body upright. Every return to the road was an act of stubbornness, not invincibility.

The new green robes of his priestly calling and a book bag carried along his travels seemed almost comically mundane beside such danger. Yet they were things he could touch, mend and keep. Not all tokens of growth needed to shine.

Sandriana was one of the names that had crossed his path in Elwynn, then appeared in his travels again. Xuthar wondered how many such brief crossings would remain only that: a glimpse of another life moving through the same world.
By the time the towers of Stormwind cast long shadows over the streets, he had learned that survival was less a great gift than a series of fragile bargains with the next moment.

pages.chapter: Chapter XX · Rain on the Road Home
pages.title: The Last Light Before Sleep
paragraphs: Stormwind had been all stone, stairs, storefronts and tall windows; the evening left its memory in the weight of small errands. Xuthar passed through shops, carried messages and attended to the concerns of people whose lives went on while kingdoms made their speeches. Among the names was Gallina's, another ordinary fragment to be kept in his ledger.

A choice made that day would outlast its coins. He set aside Herbalism and turned toward Tailoring and Enchanting, two crafts suited to a priest travelling with little: cloth to mend, and quiet power woven into objects. Fishing, too, joined his new disciplines. He could not learn every trade of the world, but he might choose those that made his hands useful.

The road bent inward again. Orange torchlight traced a stone tunnel; the way back passed guarded walkways, trees and the statues of Stormwind. He left the capital not with a triumphal procession but with the ordinary steps of a traveller who wanted somewhere to rest.

Beyond the city the weather changed. Rain drew thin bright strokes through the night. Wet cobbles led him back toward the blue roofs of Goldshire, where scattered travellers still moved beneath the lanterns. The world had not become less dangerous; it had only grown quieter.

He returned to the Lion's Pride Inn. Upstairs, beneath the soft blue canopy of a bed, the weight of the day finally settled across him. He was not thinking of glory. He was thinking of the comfort of a roof and the kindness of having survived long enough to sleep.

The silence after the day's noise was almost a language. He remembered the guard beside the water, the dust of Fargodeep Mine, the smell of ink and merchants' counters, and the deep canals beneath Stormwind's bridges. Somewhere outside, rain kept falling. He did not need to remember every word spoken that day to understand why he would rise again.
The Last Witness closed his eyes. Tomorrow could remain unwritten until it came.

pages.chapter: Chapter XX · Rain on the Road Home
pages.title: The Room Above the Common Fire
paragraphs: The city's shops and canals faded behind him as the road bent toward Elwynn. His hands had learned new work: to draw thread through cloth, to set quiet enchantments into objects, to cast a line into still water. Herbalism, for a while a possible path, he had set aside. A traveller could not carry every life he might have lived.

Rain followed him beyond the stone and into the trees. Torches burned along the guarded paths, their reflections trembling on wet ground. The statues at the great bridge gave way to the familiar shapes of Goldshire, where travellers still crossed the village in the late hour.

Upstairs at the Lion's Pride Inn, Xuthar lay beneath a blue canopy and listened to the world settle around him. Somewhere below, the common room still breathed with conversation and the scrape of chairs. He thought of the valleys, the mine, and the city that had stood between this bed and the morning.
He had saved no kingdom. He had remembered a few more names. On this first long night, that was enough.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXI · The Morning after Rain
pages.title: Three Roads Still Calling
paragraphs: The rain had accompanied him home, and the memory of it seemed to linger in the room even after the morning light returned. Xuthar woke with the peculiar weariness of a man who had travelled farther in one day than he had expected of himself.

Morning brought back the unfinished responsibilities of the road: Jasperlode's uncertain tunnels, two rare books that had gone missing, and Marshal Dughan's concerns that must be carried to Guard Thomas. Xuthar had slept, but the world had not ceased asking for help.

Jasperlode's dark tunnels waited in the distance. Two books remained unfound: Geomancy for Curious Young Wizards and Arcane Explainer: Magical Stuff in Simple Words. Their names sounded absurdly cheerful for works that had somehow found their way into danger. Elsewhere, Guard Thomas still awaited the word of Marshal Dughan.
Not every summons asks for strength, Xuthar thought. Some ask for attention; others for the patience to arrive.
He fastened the ledger and stepped toward daylight. A journey did not always announce its next trial. More often it waited, patient and ordinary, beyond the first bend.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXI · The Morning after Rain
pages.title: Three Unanswered Calls
paragraphs: Morning did not return the forest to innocence. Beyond the last houses of Goldshire, the Jasperlode Mine waited in the hills, its passages promising more darkness than a priest could measure from the road. He had already learned what a mine could take from an unprepared traveller.

Two rare books had become objects of a different search: Geomancy for Curious Young Wizards and the wonderfully solemn Arcane Explainer: Magical Stuff in Simple Words. Their names amused him; the thought of books lost to danger did not.

Marshal Dughan's concerns drew his thoughts toward Guard Thomas, somewhere in the reaches of Elwynn. Three directions, three reasons to leave the warmth behind. Xuthar fastened his satchel and listened to the day beginning outside.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXII · Where the Lake Holds Its Secrets
pages.title: Nets Beneath the Water
paragraphs: The rain of the previous night was only a memory on the road out of Goldshire. By afternoon Xuthar was standing beside a pale canvas tent and a small fire. Other travellers wandered through the trees; Sam Sarsparilla stood at the entrance to the camp. The priest had not yet found a reason to hurry.

A small camera charm now accompanied his travels, a means of holding a scene in memory when words would not come. Xuthar glanced once at the curious device, then turned his attention back to the trees. He had carried too many forgotten names to trust any single way of remembering.

At Crystal Lake, water opened under the autumn-coloured trees. The dock was busy with anglers and visitors; Lee Brown stood by the boards. Two new troubles drew Xuthar's attention: fish left half-eaten in the shallows, and small pieces of bright refuse scattered where they should not have been. Someone needed them gathered, and the shore offered no easy answers.

Xuthar cast his line along the grassy shore. The bobbers lay across the shallows, and other fishers watched the water. For a while the world was all reeds, wood and little circles spreading on the lake.

But the shores were no refuge from danger. A murloc emerged before him, its ragged silhouette breaking the peaceful picture of the lake. Xuthar had already gathered a little of the curious rubbish and a few fragments of fish; his training with the fishing line had begun to find its rhythm. Enchanting and Tailoring, however, still waited on his patient work.

Once, facing two murlocs, he barely escaped with the smallest remnant of his strength. The Streamrunners, creatures of the water's edge, had also taught him the price of a moment's carelessness. He did not know whether the lake was warning him away or demanding that he learn to listen.

Even a stolen scrap or a half-eaten fish might become testimony: a tiny remnant of what somebody had done, carried away by the current. Xuthar stood by the lake, fished, gathered what he could and faced the danger before him. He had not come to demand that the water reveal everything at once.
When he left the shore, the water kept its remaining secrets.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXII · Where the Lake Holds Its Secrets
pages.title: The Lake and Its Unclaimed Things
paragraphs: Outside Goldshire, a canvas tent and a small campfire stood among the trees. Sam Sarsparilla was nearby, another name in the great living inventory of Elwynn. Xuthar paused in the gathering warmth, then followed the road toward Crystal Lake.

The lake lay quiet beneath the branches. Lee Brown stood near the fishing dock, while other visitors cast their lines and waited for the water to answer. Xuthar joined them, the line drifting across the shallows as the world narrowed to ripples and reeds.

The shore carried its own troubles. Murlocs prowled the water; half-eaten fish and glittering pieces of rubbish seemed to tell of a place unsettled by careless hands and hungry creatures. Xuthar gathered what he could, and the work of learning to fish drew closer to completion.

The patient hours beside the water offered a different lesson from the mines. He could not command the lake, only approach it. He wondered whether the people who lived nearby had learned the same truth long before he arrived.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXII · Where the Lake Holds Its Secrets
pages.title: Three Breaths from the Water
paragraphs: The murlocs did not care whether the intruder wore priestly cloth or carried a ledger of dead names. Their weapons were crude, their movements sudden, and the water made poor footing for a man already tired from travelling.

At one terrible moment Xuthar escaped two attackers with scarcely three breaths out of a hundred left to him. He had known the brink in the vineyards and beneath the mines. He recognized it now by the same cold sensation: a world growing too large for the body entrusted to him.
The creatures of the lake had also brought him the humiliation of defeat. He would not give those moments the grandeur of martyrdom. Fear was more honest than that.
When he looked back at the wavering reeds, he felt no triumph. He felt the frightening sweetness of still being able to walk away.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXIII · The River Keeps No Footprints
pages.title: Beyond the Shimmering Water
paragraphs: The small victories of Crystal Lake had not emptied the forest of its riddles. A new errand asked him to collect vials of animal blood and Duskweed petals, such ordinary and unsettling things to gather for a stranger's purpose. He carried one vial already; the petals still waited beneath the trees.

Other obligations followed him: the crafts of Enchanting and Tailoring, Jasperlode Mine to scout, rare books to find and Guard Thomas still waiting for the word of Marshal Dughan. The ledger offered no easy order in which to honour them all.

The road yielded to water. Xuthar stepped into a broad stream while afternoon light scattered into amber along the surface. The current lifted the hem of his robe. He felt the pull of the river and kept moving.
Beyond the shallows, tall branches enclosed the way again. A forest spider waited between the trunks, a patient part of the woodland that needed no priest to explain its presence.

A river was the one page that erased its writing as soon as it was made. He left no footprint in the water, and yet the crossing had changed the day. Somewhere beyond the trees another name might be waiting to be remembered.
The last trees held the light for a moment, then let the evening deepen. Xuthar walked on, the scent of wet earth following him.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXIII · The River Keeps No Footprints
pages.title: A Vial, a Petal, a Crossing
paragraphs: An unusual errand now drew him beyond the lake: vials of animal blood, Duskweed petals and the questions such ingredients invited. The work belonged to a world where remedies and poisons could begin with the same plant, and Xuthar had not yet learned how to distinguish every good intention from a dangerous bargain.

He moved through broad water while the afternoon sun turned the current to copper. The river touched the hem of his robe and erased his footprints as quickly as he made them. For a while there was nothing but his breathing, the light, and the weight of an unfinished task.

Beyond the river the trees gathered closer. A forest spider waited among the trunks, still as a mark on a page. Xuthar did not approach every creature as an enemy. Some were simply part of the world he hoped to understand.

Behind him lay the fishing dock and the half-answered requests of Crystal Lake. Ahead waited books, mines, craftwork and a messenger's duty. The river carried neither his doubts nor his unfinished promises away.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXIII · The River Keeps No Footprints
pages.title: What the River Refused to Return
paragraphs: The stream carried all manner of small, neglected things: fish that had fed another creature, bright scraps of lost belongings, and the roots of plants whose names were spoken only when somebody needed them.

Xuthar bent at the water's edge and saw fragments of sky trembling across the current. The things gathered there seemed too small to deserve a place in history: the remains of an interrupted meal, a glimmer of forgotten silver, and dark flowers rooted in the wet earth.

But the lake had no opinion of worthiness. It held what fell into it: the remnants of meals, the glitter of lost possessions, roots that tasted the mud. The priest wondered which of those things had once been precious to someone. An object became important, he thought, the moment a person began looking for it.

He imagined gathering each small testimony carefully rather than merely ticking a count. The six trinkets, the fish, the vials and the petals belonged to different errands, but each asked the same question: what do people leave behind when they cross a place and cannot remain there?

The water did not answer. It never had. Xuthar rose, dried the edges of his journal and decided to keep asking. A witness, after all, was not someone who knew everything. A witness was someone who refused to stop looking.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXIII · The River Keeps No Footprints
pages.title: Ten Threads across Elwynn
paragraphs: As afternoon leaned toward evening, his obligations multiplied into ten different roads. The young lovers of the Stonefield and Maclure families needed help; Elmore had an errand awaiting him; a message sought Gryan Stoutmantle beyond the forests of Elwynn. Goldtooth guarded a necklace, and the boar called Princess had become an unexpected source of danger.

His work with Tailoring and Enchanting remained unfinished. The Jasperlode Mine and its dark passages still called, as did the pair of rare books and the message meant for Guard Thomas. The needs of other people multiplied faster than Xuthar could answer them.
By then he had climbed another stage of his apprenticeship, his ninth. Yet the growing strength in his hands did not solve the problem of choosing where those hands were needed most.
He closed the ledger and looked toward the west. A name on a map was not a place he had walked. There was still a long way between a summons and the journey itself.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXIV · Between the Houses
pages.title: An Unseen Road Between Two Houses
paragraphs: Two households in Elwynn had guarded an old bitterness so long that their children had inherited it like a boundary wall. Love found a way to grow between the stones, and almost immediately the world asked it to hide.

Every path across the Stonefield and Maclure lands ended at some invisible boundary. No one could agree where the old resentment had begun, but everyone knew exactly where it must be defended. The young were expected to honour a feud they had never chosen.

Xuthar came to know the names Maybell and Tommy Joe through a trail of small requests: a note, an elder's advice, a little kelp and an apothecary's peculiar preparation. Individually they were nothing remarkable. Together they formed a map of stubborn, human hope.

The invisibility liquor promised no reconciliation. It could only grant a little time in which two young people might meet without being seen. Xuthar found the idea both sad and tender: that affection should have to borrow the power of magic simply to walk down a road.

He recorded no ending for the lovers. Whether their families softened, whether the night remained kind, whether courage lasted until morning—those were stories that only they could tell. The priest closed his notebook and wrote beneath their names: 'A love that must hide is still a light.'

pages.chapter: Chapter XXV · Ten Steps Toward the Light
pages.title: The Tenth Threshold
paragraphs: By the evening of the second day, Xuthar had crossed the tenth threshold of his apprenticeship. No trumpet sounded for him. No great bell rang over Elwynn to announce that another novice had grown a little stronger.

He had come through wolves and thieves, the raw stone of mines, the dangers of murloc waters and the long paved roads to Stormwind. Some encounters had ended in success; others had dropped him helpless before the world. All of them had left marks deeper than the numbers by which travellers measured themselves.

He remembered the first gathering at Northshire Abbey, the warmth of the Lion's Pride hearth, and the rain on the road home. Each memory belonged to a different version of the same man: the uncertain arrival, the frightened survivor, the patient keeper of names.

He opened the Morvayne ledger. Its old warning was still there, written in fading letters: The last witness must not remember. Xuthar traced the words with one finger and thought of all he would have lost by obeying them.
Ten thresholds were only a beginning. Beyond them lay lives not yet met, roads not yet walked, a darkness he was still learning to question. He dipped his pen and began another page.

pages.chapter: Epilogue · The Unwritten Road
pages.title: What the Next Dawn May Bring
paragraphs: At the edge of the latest page, the ink thinned. Xuthar sat with the ledger open, his belongings close at hand, listening to distant footsteps and the restless sounds of a world that had never waited for any one man.

Somewhere beyond Elwynn a western road turned toward unfamiliar fields. In the east, old mines held their darkness. And scattered between those distant places were people who had yet to know his name, though one day their stories might be written beside his.
He did not call the empty pages a failure. A life was not complete because it had been neatly described. It was complete only when its last road had truly ended, and he had not reached that road.
Xuthar closed the book gently. The last witness was still alive. That was enough to promise another chapter.

volumes.title: The Keeper of Unmarked Trails
volumes.subtitle: The Seventh Cairn
volumes.name: Thorgar Ironbeard
volumes.motto: Measure twice. Leave no one behind.

pages.chapter: Front matter
pages.title: For the ones who will follow
paragraphs: Some maps are made to claim land. The best ones are made so another traveller can find the way home.

Thorgar Ironbeard has not yet begun his journey in Forever. What follows is the personal fiction that will travel in his pack when his time arrives. His real achievements, companions and routes are still unwritten.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Ironforge
pages.title: Brass, ink and stubbornness
paragraphs: Thorgar's childhood smelled of metal polish, fresh paper and the sharp warmth of a forge. His family repaired instruments for people who left Ironforge with hopes too large for their pockets. He learned to measure twice, not because his father feared mistakes, but because strangers might trust the work.
His mother preserved ledgers and maps with a severity the boy understood only years later. Every corrected distance meant a stranger might arrive before nightfall.
The mountain raised him, but every departing caravan taught him that the world had more corners than a well-made map could contain.
pages.caption: Illustrative Ironforge archive.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The survey
pages.title: Six stones, seven signatures
paragraphs: In an old drawer he found a survey that listed six stone cairns and carried seven names. The last signature had been scraped away. Someone had written a warning on the edge: Do not count the seventh.

Thorgar asked for an explanation and was given three different stories. His father called the document damaged; an older relative said the expedition had ended safely. Nobody seemed eager to compare their memories.
He took the family's brass compass to his workbench. Its needle would not settle where the others did. He cleaned it, checked it, and refused to call it enchanted merely because it was inconvenient.
pages.caption: Atmospheric road illustration · Fictional survey.

pages.chapter: Prologue · The Seventh Cairn
pages.title: Where the seventh stone should be
paragraphs: There are things a mountain keeps better than a man: cold, silence, and the weight of a promise made too long ago.

Six cairns on the route. Seven signatures beneath. One scratched away until the paper nearly broke. My father saw me count them, set down his hammer, and said some trails were best left to the weather.
Perhaps the compass is broken. Perhaps my pride is. I have packed my rifle and enough supplies for a poor start; I will trust neither a map nor a rumor until the ground has had its say.
For now I shall count seven stones, though I have only ever seen six.

pages.chapter: Reserved
pages.title: A road not yet walked
paragraphs: The first real chapter will begin when Thorgar is actually played. Until then, his route, pet, friends, profession progress and choices remain unknown.
Xuthar Morvayne remains the main character whose Chronicle will grow first.

volumes.title: The Listener Between Winds
volumes.subtitle: The Song of Five Leaves
volumes.name: Aelyndra Zephyrveil
volumes.motto: The wind belongs to no hand.

pages.chapter: Front matter
pages.title: To everything that must change
paragraphs: A place can be loved without being possessed. A song can be remembered without being forced to return.
Aelyndra's life in Forever remains ahead of her. Her faction, journeys and discoveries are not decided in these pages. They belong to future play, not the author's convenience.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Above the clouds
pages.title: The garden on Zephras Isle
paragraphs: The gardens of Zephras Isle demanded gentle hands. Aelyndra grew among terraces where plants leaned toward the sun and the wind could interrupt the most careful work. Her mother taught her to bind young stems without constricting them.
She was fascinated less by the breadth of the sky than by the lives that persisted beneath it. A seed that survived a storm seemed as extraordinary as any ancestral tale.
When her people argued about their future, Aelyndra tried to hear what was being said beneath the anger: the fear of losing a home, and the fear of never being allowed to leave it.
pages.caption: Landscape from the Chronicles gallery; personal scenes are fictional.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The still morning
pages.title: The fifth leaf
paragraphs: A silver chime of five leaves hung outside the family dwelling. Its notes had accompanied ordinary mornings for as long as Aelyndra remembered. One day all the plants moved in the breeze, but the chime made no sound.
She examined the hinges and cords. Nothing seemed broken. She could not prove the object meant anything beyond its own silence.
That evening she wrapped it in cloth. The island had greater troubles than an heirloom, but she suspected people first learned to recognize loss through the smallest absences.
pages.caption: Atmospheric archive illustration · Fictional family chime.

pages.chapter: Prologue · The Silent Chime
pages.title: The hour of still air
paragraphs: Some mornings the terraces sang before the sun reached them. The wind moved through chimes, leaves and narrow spaces between stone. Every sound seemed to be its own language.

Mother told me I had confused listening with naming. A thing did not become mine because I could describe it. Then the silver chime fell silent, and I understood how quickly affection can become a demand.
I have folded away my herbs and wrapped the five leaves in cloth. Soon I shall travel into a world whose winds do not know my name. I hope I will be wise enough not to demand that they learn it.
If the song returns, I would like to hear it without mistaking it for a command.

pages.chapter: Reserved
pages.title: The world beneath the clouds
paragraphs: Aelyndra's actual faction, adventures, encounters and skills will appear only once you play her in Forever.
Her personal lore is prepared, but Xuthar's chronicle comes first.
